Loss Functions and Gradient Descent

A loss function turns a model's errors on a set of examples into one number, such as mean squared error for numeric targets or log loss for predicted probabilities. Gradient descent lowers that number by repeatedly moving every parameter a small step in the direction that reduces the loss fastest, with the size of the step set by the learning rate.

1Overview

Why it matters

Linear regression has a formula for its best coefficients. Almost nothing else does. Logistic regression, matrix factorization for recommendations, every neural network and every large language model are fitted by this loop or a close variant of it: compute a loss, compute its gradient, step, repeat. Whoever trains or fine-tunes a model is choosing a loss function, a batch size and a learning rate, whether or not they set them by hand.

Those choices decide whether a training run works. A learning rate that is too high can turn the loss into nan within a few steps. One that is too low makes a job that should take an hour run for a day and stop early at a worse model. Features left on their raw scales can cause both problems at once. The wrong loss optimises the wrong thing: a classifier trained on squared error is barely punished for being confidently wrong. None of these failures raises an exception. They show up only in the loss curve, so ML engineers, data scientists and anyone who has to judge whether a training job is healthy need to read that curve and know which setting each shape points to.

Before you start

  • Calculus for ML (Derivatives and Gradients)Beginner
  • Linear RegressionBeginner

What you will be able to do

  • Compute mean squared error and log loss by hand for a few predictions and say what each one punishes.
  • Write the gradient-descent update for a linear model and reproduce two steps of it with pen and paper.
  • Compare batch, stochastic and mini-batch gradient descent by updates per epoch, cost per update and noise.
  • Predict from the curvature of a loss whether a learning rate will converge, overshoot or diverge, and confirm it in code.
  • Choose a stopping rule and say what it can miss.
  • Diagnose a failing training run from the shape of its loss curve and name the first thing to change.

Key terms

Loss function
A formula that turns a model's predictions and the true answers into one number that is lower when the predictions are better. Training searches for the parameters that minimise it.
Mean squared error (MSE)
The average of the squared differences between predictions and targets. It is the usual loss when the target is a number.
Log loss (binary cross-entropy)
The average of minus the logarithm of the probability the model gave to the label that actually occurred. It is the usual loss when the model outputs a probability.
Gradient
The list of slopes of the loss, one per parameter. Each slope says how fast the loss rises when that parameter increases and the others stay fixed.
Learning rate
The number that multiplies the gradient to give the size of each update. It is chosen by the person training the model, not learned from the data.
Batch size
The number of training examples used to compute the gradient for one update.
Epoch
One pass over the whole training set. With n examples and batches of B, an epoch contains n divided by B updates.
Stochastic gradient descent (SGD)
Gradient descent in which each update uses one randomly chosen example, or in common usage a small random batch, instead of the whole training set.
Convergence
The state in which further updates no longer reduce the loss by a meaningful amount.
Learning-rate schedule
A rule that changes the learning rate during training, for example dividing it by ten at fixed epochs or shrinking it a little after every update.

2Explanation

Introduction

In linear regression you found the best line through six deliveries by solving equations: y^=6+2.5x\hat{y} = 6 + 2.5xy^​=6+2.5x, exact, in one step. That shortcut exists because squared error on a linear model is a simple bowl with a formula for its lowest point. Change the model to a logistic regression or a neural network, or grow the data to billions of rows, and the formula is gone or too expensive. What remains is a procedure that works for almost any model: measure how wrong the model is, find out which way to nudge each parameter to make it less wrong, nudge, and repeat.

Two ideas make that procedure precise. A loss function turns "how wrong" into one number computed from the predictions and the true answers; lower is better. Gradient descent is the nudging rule. The gradient of the loss lists, for every parameter, how fast the loss rises when that parameter increases, so moving each parameter the opposite way lowers the loss. How far to move is set by a number you choose, the learning rate.

A walker coming down a hill in fog does the same thing. They cannot see the valley, but they can feel which way the ground slopes under their feet, take a step downhill and feel again. Small steps are safe and slow. Big steps are fast until one of them carries the walker across the valley and up the other side.

Here is the smallest possible case. Take one parameter www and the loss L(w)=(w−3)2L(w) = (w - 3)^2L(w)=(w−3)2, whose lowest point is at w=3w = 3w=3. Its slope is 2(w−3)2(w - 3)2(w−3). Start at w=0w = 0w=0, where the slope is −6-6−6: the loss falls as www grows. With a learning rate of 0.1 the update is w←0−0.1×(−6)=0.6w \leftarrow 0 - 0.1 \times (-6) = 0.6w←0−0.1×(−6)=0.6. The slope there is −4.8-4.8−4.8, so the next step is smaller and lands on 1.08, then 1.464, each step closing a fifth of the remaining gap to 3.

This lesson covers the two loss functions you will meet first, mean squared error and log loss; the three ways to feed data to the update (all of it, one example, or a small batch); how the learning rate decides between converging, crawling and blowing up; how to tell when training has finished; and how to recognise a failing run from its loss curve. The worked example retrains the delivery model by gradient descent and arrives at the same 6+2.5x6 + 2.5x6+2.5x.

How it works

A loss function scores the predictions

A loss function takes the model's predictions and the true targets and returns one number. Training searches for the parameters that make that number small, so the loss must respond smoothly when a parameter changes. Accuracy does not: nudging a weight usually flips no prediction, the score stays flat, and a flat score has no slope to follow.

Mean squared error (MSE) is the usual loss when the target is a number:

MSE=1n∑i=1n(y^i−yi)2\text{MSE} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} (\hat{y}_i - y_i)^2MSE=n1​i=1∑n​(y^​i​−yi​)2

It is the least-squares quantity from linear regression divided by nnn. Squaring makes one miss of 10 cost as much as a hundred misses of 1, which is why, as Google's crash course (opens in a new tab) puts it, MSE moves the model towards outliers more than mean absolute error does.

Log loss (binary cross-entropy) is the usual loss when the model outputs a probability ppp that the label yyy is 1. It is the loss the crash course (opens in a new tab) gives for logistic regression:

Log loss=−1n∑i=1n[ yiln⁡pi+(1−yi)ln⁡(1−pi) ]\text{Log loss} = -\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \big[\, y_i \ln p_i + (1 - y_i) \ln (1 - p_i) \,\big]Log loss=−n1​i=1∑n​[yi​lnpi​+(1−yi​)ln(1−pi​)]

Only one of the two terms is active for each example, so an example's loss is −ln⁡-\ln−ln of the probability the model gave to what really happened. Saying 0.9 for something that happened costs 0.105, saying 0.5 costs 0.693, and saying 0.01 costs 4.605. Squared error on a probability can never exceed 1. Log loss has no ceiling, and that is what makes a confident wrong answer so expensive.

For labels 1, 0, 1, 0 and predictions 0.9, 0.2, 0.6, 0.99 the four losses are 0.105, 0.223, 0.511 and 4.605. Their mean is 1.361, and 85% of it comes from the one confident miss. Log loss is the negative log-likelihood of the labels under the model's probabilities, as scikit-learn's reference (opens in a new tab) defines it, so minimising it is the maximum-likelihood fitting described in probability for ML.

The gradient and the update rule

For a linear model y^=wx+b\hat{y} = wx + by^​=wx+b trained with MSE, the chain rule gives

∂L∂w=2n∑i=1n(y^i−yi) xi,∂L∂b=2n∑i=1n(y^i−yi)\frac{\partial L}{\partial w} = \frac{2}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} (\hat{y}_i - y_i)\, x_i, \qquad \frac{\partial L}{\partial b} = \frac{2}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} (\hat{y}_i - y_i)∂w∂L​=n2​i=1∑n​(y^​i​−yi​)xi​,∂b∂L​=n2​i=1∑n​(y^​i​−yi​)

For a logistic model p=σ(wx+b)p = \sigma(wx + b)p=σ(wx+b) trained with log loss the result has the same shape without the 2: 1n∑(pi−yi) xi\frac{1}{n}\sum (p_i - y_i)\,x_in1​∑(pi​−yi​)xi​ and 1n∑(pi−yi)\frac{1}{n}\sum (p_i - y_i)n1​∑(pi​−yi​). In both cases each example pushes a weight in proportion to its error times its input. With all parameters collected in a vector θ\thetaθ and a learning rate η\etaη, one step of gradient descent is

θ←θ−η ∇L(θ)\theta \leftarrow \theta - \eta \, \nabla L(\theta)θ←θ−η∇L(θ)
python
def gradient_step(w, b, xs, ys, lr):
    """One gradient-descent step for y = w*x + b under mean squared error."""
    errors = [w * x + b - y for x, y in zip(xs, ys)]
    grad_w = 2 * sum(e * x for e, x in zip(errors, xs)) / len(xs)
    grad_b = 2 * sum(errors) / len(xs)
    return w - lr * grad_w, b - lr * grad_b

For models with many layers the gradient comes from backpropagation, and a framework computes it for you. The update itself is unchanged, as the training loop in PyTorch fundamentals shows.

Batch, stochastic and mini-batch

The formulas above average over all nnn examples. The three variants differ only in how many examples go into each gradient.

VariantExamples per updateUpdates per epochBehaviour
Batchall nnn1Exact gradient and a smooth loss curve; every update costs a full pass over the data
Stochastic (SGD)1nnnCheap, frequent, noisy updates; the loss goes up as well as down
Mini-batchBBB, commonly 50 to 256n/Bn / Bn/BNoise shrinks as BBB grows, and a batch is computed as one vectorised operation

An epoch is one pass over the training set. With 1,000 examples and 20 epochs, the crash course (opens in a new tab) counts 20 updates for full batch, 20,000 for SGD and 200 for mini-batches of 100. A gradient computed from a random sample points, on average, the same way as the full gradient. What varies is the scatter around it, and its standard deviation falls only with the square root of the batch size, as Dive into Deep Learning (opens in a new tab) notes: four times the batch costs four times the computation and halves the noise. Shuffle the data every epoch so that each batch is a fair sample. The 50 to 256 range in the table is the one Ruder's overview (opens in a new tab) gives as common. Libraries call all three variants "SGD", because an SGD optimizer applies the same update to whatever batch it is handed.

The learning rate

Near a minimum a loss looks like a bowl. If the bowl's curvature (second derivative) along some direction is hhh, one step multiplies the distance to the bottom along that direction by (1−ηh)(1 - \eta h)(1−ηh). Three regimes follow:

  • η<1/h\eta < 1/hη<1/h: the distance shrinks steadily. Very small values waste steps.
  • 1/h<η<2/h1/h < \eta < 2/h1/h<η<2/h: every step overshoots to the other side but lands closer.
  • η>2/h\eta > 2/hη>2/h: every step lands further away, and the loss grows until it overflows.

For f(x)=x2f(x) = x^2f(x)=x2, where h=2h = 2h=2, starting from x=10x = 10x=10: ten steps at η=0.2\eta = 0.2η=0.2 reach 0.06, at 0.05 only 3.49, and at 1.1 the iterate has grown to 61.9. These are the three cases shown in Dive into Deep Learning (opens in a new tab).

A model has many directions with different curvatures. The steepest one sets the ceiling on η\etaη, and the flattest one then decides how long training takes, because its factor (1−ηh)(1 - \eta h)(1−ηh) sits just below

  1. Features on very different scales create exactly that mismatch, which is why scikit-learn (opens in a new tab) lists sensitivity to feature scaling among SGD's disadvantages and why scaling features comes before gradient descent. A schedule changes the rate during training. With noisy gradients a constant rate leaves the parameters jittering around the minimum, and lowering the rate over time (step decay, exponential decay or 1/t1/t1/t decay in the CS231n notes (opens in a new tab)) lets them settle. Optimizers such as momentum and Adam, covered in training deep networks, change how the step is built from recent gradients. They still need a base learning rate, and everything in this section applies to it.

Convergence and stopping

Training has converged when further updates no longer reduce the loss by a meaningful amount. Practical stopping rules are a minimum improvement per epoch, a cap on the number of epochs, and early stopping when the loss on held-out data stops improving. Real systems expose exactly these settings: BigQuery ML (opens in a new tab) stops at the first iteration that improves the loss by less than 1% unless told otherwise, and scikit-learn's SGD estimators by default stop when the training loss has failed to improve by tol for n_iter_no_change epochs in a row.

For linear and logistic regression the loss is convex, a single bowl, so the point where gradient descent settles is the global minimum; the crash course's page on gradient descent (opens in a new tab) plots that surface for a linear model. Neural-network losses are not convex, and Ruder's overview (opens in a new tab) names saddle points and the plateaus around them, where the gradient is close to zero in every direction, as the harder obstacle. A flat loss curve therefore says only that the gradient is small where the parameters are now. It does not say that the model is the best one available.

Reading a failing run

Plot the training loss against updates and the validation loss against epochs. Most failures show one of a few shapes.

Two cheap checks before a long run catch most bugs. The first loss should match what an uninformed model gives (ln⁡2=0.693\ln 2 = 0.693ln2=0.693 for binary log loss at p=0.5p = 0.5p=0.5), and the model should be able to drive the loss to almost zero on a handful of examples. The CS231n notes recommend both.

Step 4: run it

Plain Python, no packages:

python
import random

km      = [2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12]
minutes = [13, 12, 23, 25, 33, 35]

def mse(w, b, xs):
    return sum((w * x + b - y) ** 2 for x, y in zip(xs, minutes)) / len(xs)

def descend(xs, lr, epochs, batch_size=6, decay=0.0):
    """Gradient descent on MSE from w = b = 0. batch_size 6 is batch, 1 is stochastic."""
    rng = random.Random(0)
    w, b, updates = 0.0, 0.0, 0
    for _ in range(epochs):
        order = list(range(len(xs)))
        rng.shuffle(order)                             # new order every epoch
        for start in range(0, len(xs), batch_size):
            rows = order[start:start + batch_size]
            errors = [w * xs[i] + b - minutes[i] for i in rows]
            grad_w = 2 * sum(e * xs[i] for e, i in zip(errors, rows)) / len(rows)
            grad_b = 2 * sum(errors) / len(rows)
            step = lr / (1 + decay * updates)          # decay=0 keeps the rate constant
            w, b, updates = w - step * grad_w, b - step * grad_b, updates + 1
    return w, b

def report(label, xs, w, b):
    print(f"{label:<28} w={w:9.4f} b={b:9.4f} loss={mse(w, b, xs):.4f}")

for lr, epochs in [(0.01, 100), (0.01, 5000), (0.02, 10)]:
    report(f"raw km, lr={lr}, {epochs} steps", km, *descend(km, lr, epochs))

mean = sum(km) / 6
std = (sum((x - mean) ** 2 for x in km) / 6) ** 0.5
z = [(x - mean) / std for x in km]
for lr, epochs in [(0.1, 2), (0.1, 50), (0.5, 1), (1.05, 20)]:
    report(f"scaled, lr={lr}, {epochs} steps", z, *descend(z, lr, epochs))

w, b = descend(z, 0.1, 50)
print(f"back in km: slope={w / std:.4f} intercept={b - w * mean / std:.4f}")

for label, size, decay in [("batch of 6, 30 updates", 6, 0), ("batches of 2, 90 updates", 2, 0),
                           ("one row, 180 updates", 1, 0), ("one row, decaying rate", 1, 0.05)]:
    report(label, z, *descend(z, 0.1, 30, size, decay))

Step 5: read the result

  • Unscaled, the run crawls or explodes. At 0.01 the slope is 2.95 after 100 steps (the answer is 2.5) and the intercept is at 2.15, not 6, so 5,000 steps are needed. At 0.02, just above the limit of 0.0163, the loss passes a million in ten steps.
  • Scaled, 50 steps are enough, and converting back gives the least-squares line 6+2.5x6 + 2.5x6+2.5x. At η=0.5=1/h\eta = 0.5 = 1/hη=0.5=1/h a single step lands on the minimum; at 1.05>2/h1.05 > 2/h1.05>2/h the run diverges.
  • Smaller batches make more updates per epoch but do not settle. After the same 30 epochs the one-row run sits at 5.38 because each row's own gradient is not zero at the minimum, so every step knocks the parameters off it. Shrinking the rate as training proceeds brings it to 5.0003.

Edge cases and limitations

Log loss with a predicted probability of exactly 0 or 1
The logarithm of 0 is minus infinity, so a single example predicted with probability 0 for the label that occurred makes the mean loss infinite, and automatic differentiation through a separate sigmoid and logarithm then returns NaN gradients. This happens in practice when a sigmoid saturates in floating point. scikit-learn's log_loss clips probabilities to the range from eps to 1 − eps, where eps is the machine precision, which keeps the result finite. In your own code clip the probabilities, or better, compute the loss from the raw score before the sigmoid, which deep learning libraries offer as a "with logits" loss.
Perfectly separable classes have no minimum to converge to
If a line separates the two classes without error, log loss can always be lowered a little more by making the weights larger, so the loss creeps towards 0 and the weights grow without bound. Training ends only because a stopping rule fires, and the weights depend on when it did. The sign is a training loss that keeps shrinking while the weight norm keeps growing. Google's crash course calls regularisation, by an L2 penalty or early stopping, critical for logistic regression because the loss would otherwise keep being driven towards 0.
A relative-improvement stopping rule can fire in a slow valley
On the unscaled delivery data with a learning rate of 0.01, the loss falls from 630.17 to 10.93 in four steps and then improves by only 0.45% on the fifth. A rule that stops below 1% improvement ends training there with a slope of 3.14, an intercept of 0.47 and a loss of 10.88, more than twice the true minimum of 5. Tightening the threshold to 0.1% stops at step 275 with the loss still at 5.75. The fix is to scale the features, not to tune the threshold.
Summing the loss over the batch instead of averaging it
If the loss is summed, the gradient grows in proportion to the batch size, and so does every step. Doubling the batch then doubles the effective learning rate, and a run that was stable at batch 32 can diverge at batch 256 with nothing else changed. The Facebook large-minibatch paper lists the distributed version among its pitfalls: normalise by the total mini-batch, not by each worker's share. Check which reduction your loss function uses before comparing learning rates across batch sizes.
One extreme target under squared error
The gradient of squared error grows in proportion to the error, so a row whose target is wrong by a factor of a thousand produces a step a thousand times larger than its neighbours. In stochastic or small-batch training that one update can throw the parameters far enough to cause divergence at a learning rate that was otherwise safe. Fix the data if the value is an error. If it is real, use a loss that grows linearly for large errors, such as the Huber loss offered by scikit-learn's SGDRegressor.

When to use it, and when something simpler is enough

Use it when

  • The model has no closed-form solution. That covers logistic regression, matrix factorization and every neural network, provided the loss is differentiable in the parameters.
  • The data is too large for a direct solver or does not fit in memory. Mini-batch updates need one batch in memory at a time, and the cost of one update does not depend on the size of the dataset.
  • Examples arrive continuously and the model has to keep learning from them, as in click prediction, where each example may be seen only once.
  • You want to continue from existing parameters, for instance a warm start on new data or fine-tuning a pre-trained network.

Think twice when

  • The problem is an ordinary least-squares fit of modest width. A direct solver returns the exact answer with no learning rate to tune. BigQuery ML's default uses the normal equation unless feature cardinality passes 10,000, rows are scarce, or L1 regularisation or a warm start is requested.
  • The thing being chosen is not a smooth parameter. Tree splits, the number of clusters and hyperparameters have no gradient, and tree learners and search methods handle them.
  • The problem is small, smooth and convex and you need a precise optimum. Second-order and quasi-Newton solvers such as L-BFGS usually get there in far fewer iterations and have no learning rate to tune.

A simpler alternative. For a linear model with squared error, solve the least-squares problem directly as in the linear regression lesson, and for other classical models use the library's default solver before writing a training loop. That stops being enough when the number of feature columns makes the direct solve too expensive (its cost grows with rows times columns squared), when the data no longer fits in memory, or when the model is not linear in its parameters.

Key takeaways

  • A loss function compresses a model's errors into one number. Mean squared error suits numeric targets and log loss suits probabilities, where a confident wrong answer costs far more than an unsure one.
  • Gradient descent repeats one update, each parameter minus the learning rate times the slope of the loss for that parameter, until the loss stops improving.
  • Batch gradient descent uses every row per update, stochastic uses one and mini-batch uses a small sample, which trades the cost of each update against the noise in its direction.
  • The learning rate must stay below 2 divided by the largest curvature of the loss or training diverges, and the smallest curvature then decides how many steps are needed.
  • Standardising the features evens out those curvatures and can cut the steps needed from thousands to dozens.
  • The loss curve is the main diagnostic. An explosion means the rate is too high, a slow straight fall means it is too low, wide jitter means the batch is too small for the rate, and a flat line does not prove a minimum.

Sources for this explanation: [1], [2], [3], [4], [5], [6], [7], [8], [9], [12]

3Real-world applications

5 documented uses of Loss Functions and Gradient Descent. Each one names the real system, the problem it solves and its tradeoff, with links to the sources.

  1. BigQuery ML: batch gradient descent or the normal equation, with a line-searched learning rate
  2. scikit-learn SGDClassifier: learning a text classifier from a stream that does not fit in memory
  3. Netflix Prize: Simon Funk's per-rating gradient steps for matrix factorization
  4. Facebook: scaling the learning rate with the mini-batch to train ImageNet in one hour
  5. Google ad click prediction: online gradient descent on log loss with a learning rate per feature

Example 1 of 5

BigQuery ML: batch gradient descent or the normal equation, with a line-searched learning rate

Google Cloud (BigQuery ML)Documented in official docs

BigQuery ML trains linear and logistic regression models inside the BigQuery data warehouse from a CREATE MODEL statement. Google's reference for generalized linear models documents the training options, the reference for the ML.TRAINING_INFO function documents what is recorded for every training iteration, and the automatic preprocessing guide documents how numeric features are scaled. [13][14][15]

The problem

A warehouse user writes SQL, not an optimiser. The service has to decide how to minimise the loss for tables that range from a few columns to one-hot encoded features numbering in the tens of thousands, choose a step size that converges without the user tuning it, and stop without being told how many passes are enough. Each training iteration is a pass over the whole training table.

Where this topic fits

The OPTIMIZE_STRATEGY option selects between the closed-form solution from the linear regression lesson (NORMAL_EQUATION) and BATCH_GRADIENT_DESCENT. When gradient descent runs, LEARN_RATE_STRATEGY decides how the learning rate is set at each iteration, and EARLY_STOP, MIN_REL_PROGRESS and MAX_ITERATIONS define when training ends. ML.TRAINING_INFO exposes the resulting loss curve.

How it is applied, step by step

  1. The user runs CREATE MODEL with MODEL_TYPE set to LINEAR_REG or LOGISTIC_REG. The loss being minimised is mean squared error for linear regression and log loss for logistic regression.
  2. Before training, BigQuery ML standardises and centres numeric columns at zero for most model types (the documented exceptions are tree-based models and k-means), so the optimiser sees features on comparable scales without the user preparing them.
  3. With the default AUTO_STRATEGY (the reference documents OPTIMIZE_STRATEGY for linear regression models), the normal equation is used unless L1 regularisation or a warm start is requested, the total cardinality of the features exceeds 10,000, or there are fewer than ten training examples per unit of cardinality. In those cases batch gradient descent is used.
  4. One iteration of batch gradient descent is one pass over the training data: the gradient of the loss is accumulated over all rows and every weight is updated once.
  5. Under the default LINE_SEARCH strategy the service tries several learning rates around the current one in each iteration and keeps the model with the lowest loss, so the rate can grow from one iteration to the next. Under CONSTANT it uses the LEARN_RATE the user supplies.
  6. After each iteration the relative improvement in the loss is compared with MIN_REL_PROGRESS. Training stops at the first iteration that improves by less than that fraction, or when MAX_ITERATIONS is reached.
  7. The user queries ML.TRAINING_INFO for the loss, evaluation loss, learning rate and duration of each iteration, and reads the curve as described in this lesson.

Why this approach fits

A full pass over a table is the natural unit of work for a SQL engine. The gradient of an averaged loss is a sum of per-row terms, which a distributed scan can aggregate without any random access to individual rows, so batch gradient descent maps directly onto what the warehouse already does well. The normal equation needs a system with one row and column per feature, which grows quadratically with the feature count; the documented switch at a cardinality of 10,000 is where the service stops using it. Line search removes the setting that users are least equipped to choose, and the automatic standardisation removes the scale mismatch that the worked example shows slowing raw features down, which is why a default rate of 0.1 is plausible without hand-scaling.

Limitation or tradeoff

Every update costs a full scan, so on a large table the model makes far fewer updates per unit of computation than mini-batch training would. With a constant learning rate, the default cap of 20 iterations can end training well short of the minimum. Line search protects against a bad rate at the price the reference states: slower training and more bytes processed. The relative-improvement rule shares the weakness described under edge cases, since it cannot tell a finished run from a slow one.

What the sources document

  • OPTIMIZE_STRATEGY, documented for linear regression models, accepts AUTO_STRATEGY (the default), BATCH_GRADIENT_DESCENT, which optimizes the loss using its gradient, and NORMAL_EQUATION, the analytical least-squares solution. AUTO_STRATEGY picks batch gradient descent when L1_REG is specified, WARM_START is TRUE, total feature cardinality is above 10,000, or examples number under ten times that cardinality, and the normal equation otherwise. [13]
  • BigQuery ML's automatic preprocessing standardizes and centers numerical columns at zero before training for most models; the documented exceptions are boosted tree and random forest models, which are not standardized, and k-means, where the STANDARDIZE_FEATURES option decides. [15]
  • LEARN_RATE_STRATEGY defaults to LINE_SEARCH, which the reference says slows down training and increases the number of bytes processed but generally converges even with a larger initial learning rate. CONSTANT uses the value of LEARN_RATE, whose default is 0.1. [13]
  • MAX_ITERATIONS defaults to 20, and one iteration is a single pass of the entire training data. EARLY_STOP defaults to TRUE and stops training after the first iteration in which the relative loss improvement is less than MIN_REL_PROGRESS, which defaults to 0.01. [13]
  • ML.TRAINING_INFO returns for each iteration the training loss (mean squared error for linear regression, log loss for logistic regression), the loss on holdout data, the learning rate and the duration. With LINE_SEARCH and an initial rate of 0.1, the first iteration compares models trained with learning rates of 0.2, 0.1, 0.05 and 0.025. [14]

The facts above come from the cited sources. The steps and analysis in this example are our explanation of how they fit together.

Example 2 of 5

scikit-learn SGDClassifier: learning a text classifier from a stream that does not fit in memory

scikit-learnDocumented in official docs

scikit-learn's SGDClassifier fits linear models by stochastic gradient descent. The user guide says where the estimators are applied, the class reference describes the partial_fit method, and the official example "Out-of-core classification of text documents" applies them to the Reuters-21578 newswire collection. [9][10][11]

The problem

A text collection can be larger than main memory, and new words keep appearing as more documents arrive. A solver that needs the whole feature matrix at once cannot be used. The example's task is a binary classifier that separates Reuters stories on the topic "acq" from all others while holding only a small slice of the collection in memory at any moment.

Where this topic fits

Mini-batch stochastic gradient descent is the learning step. Documents are parsed from disk as a stream, grouped into mini-batches, turned into sparse vectors by a HashingVectorizer, and passed to partial_fit, which runs SGD over that batch and returns. Accuracy on held-out documents is recorded after every batch.

How it is applied, step by step

  1. Take the first 1,000 documents of the stream as a test set; the example drops those that have no topic label. They are vectorised once and never used for training.
  2. Read the next 1,000 documents. This is the mini-batch, and nothing older stays in memory.
  3. Hash each document's words into a fixed space of 2^18 columns. Hashing needs no fitted vocabulary, so a word first seen in a late batch still maps to a valid column.
  4. Call partial_fit on the batch, passing the full list of classes. The estimator visits the batch's samples and, for each one, computes the gradient of its loss and moves the weights against it with the current learning rate.
  5. Score the model on the held-out documents, log the accuracy against the number of documents seen, and return to the second step until the stream ends.
  6. Because partial_fit leaves convergence to the caller, decide from that accuracy log when to stop, or pass over the stream again in a different order.

Why this approach fits

The cost of one SGD update depends on the non-zero features of one document, not on the size of the collection, and the model is a single weight per hashed column. Memory therefore stays flat however long the stream runs. Any method that needs every row for each step, whether the normal equations or batch gradient descent, would need the collection in memory or a full re-read from disk per update.

Limitation or tradeoff

The reference is explicit that one call to partial_fit does not guarantee a minimum of the cost function and that convergence checks, early stopping and learning-rate adjustments are the user's job. A stream is also not shuffled: if it is ordered by date or topic, late batches pull the weights towards themselves. The user guide adds that SGD is sensitive to feature scaling and needs its regularisation strength and number of iterations chosen.

What the sources document

  • The user guide says SGD has been successfully applied to large-scale and sparse machine learning problems often encountered in text classification and natural language processing, and that with sparse data the classifiers easily scale to problems with more than 10^5 training examples and more than 10^5 features. [9]
  • SGDClassifier is documented as estimating the gradient of the loss one sample at a time and updating the model along the way with a decreasing learning rate, and as allowing minibatch (online or out-of-core) learning through the partial_fit method. [10]
  • partial_fit performs one epoch of stochastic gradient descent on the given samples and internally uses max_iter = 1, so a minimum of the cost function is not guaranteed after one call; objective convergence, early stopping and learning-rate adjustments are left to the user. [10]
  • The out-of-core example learns from Reuters-21578 with classifiers that support partial_fit, uses a HashingVectorizer so that every batch is projected into the same feature space, feeds mini-batches of 1,000 documents so that at most 1,000 are in memory, and first holds out 1,000 documents to estimate accuracy. [11]
  • The guide warns that the training data should be shuffled and that features should ideally be standardised, lists sensitivity to feature scaling among the disadvantages of SGD, and reports that SGD empirically converges after observing approximately 10^6 training samples. [9]

The facts above come from the cited sources. The steps and analysis in this example are our explanation of how they fit together.

Example 3 of 5

Netflix Prize: Simon Funk's per-rating gradient steps for matrix factorization

Documented in an engineering article

During the Netflix Prize, a public competition to predict film ratings, Simon Funk published the method behind an entry that, after a 50/50 blend with another entrant's results, was tied for third place at the time. His December 2006 post gives the model, the update code and the constants. Koren, Bell and Volinsky's 2009 IEEE Computer article describes the same procedure as stochastic gradient descent. [16][17]

The problem

Netflix supplied about 100 million ratings of 17 thousand films by 500 thousand users and scored entries by root mean squared error on hidden ratings. Laid out as a user-by-film table, the data has about 8.5 billion cells, of which one in 85 is filled. Funk wanted to describe each user and each film by a few numbers whose products reproduce the known ratings, but a textbook singular value decomposition needs every cell and is costly at that size.

Where this topic fits

The loss is the squared error between a known rating and the product of a user value and a film value, taken over the known ratings only. Gradient descent, applied one rating at a time, replaces the matrix decomposition. It is the whole training algorithm, with a learning rate, a regularisation constant and a fixed number of epochs as its settings.

How it is applied, step by step

  1. Start from a baseline prediction built from the film's average rating and the user's average offset. Give every user and every film a value of 0.1 for the feature being trained; the prediction adds the product of the two values to the baseline.
  2. Visit one known rating and compute the error: the actual rating minus the current prediction.
  3. Differentiate the squared error with respect to the two values involved. The slope for the user value is minus the error times the film value, and the reverse for the film value, with the constant 2 absorbed into the learning rate. Move each value by the learning rate times the error times the other value.
  4. While updating, also subtract a small multiple of each value. This pulls the values of users and films with few ratings back towards zero.
  5. Repeat for every known rating. One pass over all of them is one epoch; empty cells contribute nothing and cost nothing.
  6. Stop the feature after a fixed number of epochs, chosen because the error on held-out ratings turns upward while the training error is still falling, then train the next feature on what is left.

Why this approach fits

The loss is a sum over known ratings, so its gradient is too, and one rating involves exactly two parameters of the feature being trained. A stochastic step is therefore a handful of multiplications, and the missing cells are skipped for free. Batch gradient descent would perform the same 100 million small computations to make a single update where the per-rating version makes 100 million.

Limitation or tradeoff

Koren and co-authors note that the objective is not convex because both sets of factors are unknown, and Funk reports that the starting values matter once training is stopped early. The learning rate was a lucky first guess that he says he regretted changing. Updates that depend on the previous one are hard to parallelise: the 2009 article prefers alternating least squares when the work must be spread across machines, or when feedback is implicit and looping over every training case is no longer practical.

What the sources document

  • Funk describes the data as 100 million ratings, from 1 to 5, of 17 thousand movies by 500 thousand users, which as a matrix would have about 8.5 billion entries with values given for only one in eighty-five of the cells. [16]
  • His method is to take the derivative of the approximation error with respect to the parameters and follow it, ignoring the error on the empty cells. The resulting two-line update is evaluated for each rating in the training database. [16]
  • He says he set the learning rate to 0.001 on day one and regretted every change to it, adds a regularisation constant K that, as he recalls, his collaborator Vincent liked at about 0.02, and reports that his laptop made a training pass through all 100 million ratings in about seven and a half seconds. [16]
  • Because the probe-set RMSE eventually turns upward while the training error is still falling, he trained each feature for a fixed number of epochs, about 120 for the constants given. [16]
  • Koren, Bell and Volinsky write that Simon Funk popularized a stochastic gradient descent optimization of the regularised squared-error objective: the algorithm loops through all ratings in the training set, computes each prediction error, and modifies the parameters in the opposite direction of the gradient by a magnitude proportional to a constant γ. [17]

The facts above come from the cited sources. The steps and analysis in this example are our explanation of how they fit together.

Example 4 of 5

Facebook: scaling the learning rate with the mini-batch to train ImageNet in one hour

FacebookDocumented in a paper

"Accurate, Large Minibatch SGD: Training ImageNet in 1 Hour" by Goyal and colleagues at Facebook (arXiv 1706.02677, 2017) reports how the team trained a ResNet-50 image classifier with distributed synchronous SGD on 256 GPUs. [18][19]

The problem

Training ResNet-50 on about 1.28 million ImageNet images with mini-batches of 256 took 29 hours on 8 GPUs. Splitting the work across more GPUs shortens an epoch only if the mini-batch grows with the number of GPUs. A larger mini-batch means fewer parameter updates per epoch, and with an unchanged learning rate the model ends up less accurate: the paper's Table 2a reports 41.67% top-1 error for an 8k mini-batch left at a rate of 0.1.

Where this topic fits

Two of this lesson's settings, the batch size and the learning rate, are traded against each other. Each of kkk workers computes the gradient on 32 images, and the gradients are averaged into one update for a mini-batch of 32k32k32k images. The paper's contribution is the rule for the learning rate that keeps that one large step equivalent to the many small steps it replaces, and the warmup that makes the rule safe at the start of training.

How it is applied, step by step

  1. Fix the baseline: 8 GPUs with 32 images each give a mini-batch of 256, trained with a learning rate of 0.1 for 90 epochs, dividing the rate by 10 at epochs 30, 60 and 80.
  2. Add workers. With k GPUs the mini-batch is 32k images, and every worker's gradient is averaged into one synchronous update.
  3. Scale the learning rate by the same factor as the mini-batch: 0.1 × kn / 256, which is 3.2 for a mini-batch of 8,192. The reasoning is that k small steps at rate η move the weights about as far as one step on a k-times larger batch at rate kη, as long as the gradient changes little over those k steps.
  4. That condition fails at the start of training, when the weights change quickly. So ramp the rate linearly from 0.1 to 3.2 over the first 5 epochs instead of starting at 3.2.
  5. Follow the usual schedule after the warmup and compare the validation error with the baseline's.

Why this approach fits

Averaging over more examples makes a gradient more accurate, but it does not make it larger. With a fixed rate, a 32-times larger batch therefore takes 32 times fewer steps of about the same size per epoch and covers less ground. Raising the rate in proportion restores the distance covered per epoch, and the lower noise of the large batch is what makes such a long step tolerable. Warmup deals with the one phase where the argument breaks: early on the loss surface under the weights changes quickly, and a step sized for later is too large.

Limitation or tradeoff

The paper reports that the rule holds only up to a mini-batch of about 8k on ImageNet: validation error rises to 24.79% at 16k and 27.55% at 32k. It also depends on implementation details the authors list as pitfalls, such as normalising the per-worker loss by the whole mini-batch and shuffling the data once per epoch across all workers. The constants belong to one network, one dataset and SGD with momentum; other models and optimisers need their own check.

What the sources document

  • The paper states its linear scaling rule as: when the minibatch size is multiplied by k, multiply the learning rate by k, keeping all other hyper-parameters unchanged. All models were trained for 90 epochs with a reference learning rate of 0.1 × kn / 256 (n = 32 images per worker), reduced by a factor of 10 at the 30th, 60th and 80th epoch. [19]
  • Table 2a compares learning-rate rules for an 8k minibatch: keeping the rate at 0.1 gives 41.67% top-1 validation error, the square-root rule 0.1 × √32 gives 26.22%, and the linear rule 0.1 × 32 gives 23.74%. [19]
  • The authors found that a constant low learning rate for the first 5 epochs was not sufficient for large minibatches. Their gradual warmup starts from a learning rate of η and increments it by a constant amount at each iteration so that it reaches kη after 5 epochs. [19]
  • Table 1 reports top-1 ImageNet validation error of 23.60% ± 0.12 for the 256 minibatch and 23.74% ± 0.09 for the 8k minibatch with gradual warmup, against 24.84% with no warmup and 25.88% with constant warmup. [19]
  • The abstract reports that the Caffe2-based system trains ResNet-50 with a minibatch size of 8192 on 256 GPUs in one hour while matching small minibatch accuracy. [18][19]

The facts above come from the cited sources. The steps and analysis in this example are our explanation of how they fit together.

Example 5 of 5

Google ad click prediction: online gradient descent on log loss with a learning rate per feature

GoogleDocumented in a paper

"Ad Click Prediction: a View from the Trenches" by McMahan and fifteen co-authors at Google (KDD 2013) presents case studies from the deployed system that predicts click-through rates for sponsored search advertising. [21][20]

The problem

For each query and candidate ad, the ad auction needs an estimate of the probability of a click. The paper describes predictions made many billions of times per day, feature vectors with billions of possible dimensions of which a few hundred are non-zero in any one example, and a model that has to be updated quickly as new clicks and non-clicks are observed. The training data is a stream.

Where this topic fits

The model is a logistic regression and the loss is log loss, exactly as in this lesson. Training is the stochastic end of the range taken to its limit: each example is used once, a gradient is computed from it alone, and the weights of its non-zero features are updated before the next example. The paper's refinements concern the learning rate, with one per coordinate, and sparsity, through the FTRL-Proximal algorithm.

How it is applied, step by step

  1. An example arrives as a sparse feature vector x. Predict the click probability p as the sigmoid of the dot product of the current weights and x.
  2. Observe the label y, 1 for a click and 0 otherwise. The example's log loss is −y ln p − (1 − y) ln(1 − p).
  3. The gradient of that loss with respect to the weights is (p − y) times x. It is zero for every feature absent from the example, so only a few hundred weights are touched.
  4. Move each of those weights against its gradient using its own learning rate, α / (β + √(sum of that feature's squared gradients so far)). A feature seen millions of times ends up with a small rate, and a rare one keeps a large rate.
  5. Discard the example and read the next one. A single pass over the stream is all the training there is.
  6. In the deployed system the same gradients drive FTRL-Proximal, which adds L1 regularisation so that many weights are exactly zero. Without regularisation it produces the same weights as online gradient descent.

Why this approach fits

With a noisy stream, one global learning rate has to shrink over time for the weights to settle. In this data, features differ by orders of magnitude in how often they occur, so a rate small enough for a feature present in every example barely moves a feature seen ten times. Keeping a rate per coordinate lets each weight follow its own schedule. It is a cheap, per-feature form of the curvature matching that standardising the feature provides in the worked example.

Limitation or tradeoff

Plain online gradient descent leaves almost no weight exactly zero, which the paper identifies as a memory problem and the reason for FTRL-Proximal. Per-coordinate rates need an extra accumulated number for every feature. The authors also report serious round-off problems when many tiny steps are accumulated in 32-bit floats. A rate that can only shrink reacts slowly if the meaning of a frequent feature changes.

What the sources document

  • The paper presents case studies from the deployed system used at Google to predict ad click-through rates for sponsored search, in which predictions are made many billions of times per day and the model has to be updated quickly as new clicks and non-clicks are observed. [21][20]
  • It defines the LogLoss of an example as −y log p − (1 − y) log(1 − p), with p the sigmoid of the dot product of weights and features, and gives its gradient as (p − y) times the feature vector. [21]
  • The authors note that although the feature vector might have billions of dimensions, each instance typically has only hundreds of nonzero values, and that each training example only needs to be considered once. [21]
  • Online gradient descent, which a footnote calls essentially the same as stochastic gradient descent, updates the weights by subtracting a learning rate times the gradient. The paper's per-coordinate rate is α / (β + √(sum of that coordinate's squared gradients)), with β = 1 described as usually good enough. [21]
  • In the reported experiment, per-coordinate learning rates reduced AucLoss by 11.2% compared with a global-learning-rate baseline, in a setting where the authors consider reductions of 1% large. [21]

The facts above come from the cited sources. The steps and analysis in this example are our explanation of how they fit together.

4Common mistakes

  1. Running gradient descent on features left in their raw units.

    Why it causes problems
    The feature with the largest numbers sets the largest curvature and therefore the highest learning rate that does not diverge. At that rate the weights of small-scale features and the intercept barely move, so the run either explodes or crawls for thousands of steps and is stopped at biased coefficients.
    How to recognise it
    The largest stable learning rate is tiny, such as 0.0000001. The loss drops quickly for a few steps and then flattens far above a baseline's error, and the intercept and some coefficients are still close to their starting values.
    How to fix it
    Standardise every numeric feature (subtract the mean, divide by the standard deviation) with statistics computed on the training set only, ideally inside a pipeline, and then choose the learning rate again. The usable rate is typically far larger afterwards.

  2. Picking a learning rate by guesswork and keeping it without looking at the loss curve.

    Why it causes problems
    A rate ten times too small can look like a model that has stopped learning, and a rate slightly too large can look like a noisy but working run. Both waste the whole training budget and end at a worse model than a five-minute sweep would have found.
    How to recognise it
    There is no plot of training loss against updates, or the plot shows a slow straight line, a loss that falls and then stalls high, or values that jump to inf or NaN.
    How to fix it
    Run short trials at rates spaced by factors of about three (0.001, 0.003, 0.01 and so on), plot the loss for each, and take the largest rate whose curve falls smoothly. Repeat whenever the batch size, the feature scaling or the model changes.

  3. Judging convergence from the loss of individual mini-batches.

    Why it causes problems
    A mini-batch loss is a noisy estimate that goes up as often as it goes down near the end of training. Stopping the first time it rises ends training early, and waiting for it to stop moving never ends it. The stopping point then depends on the random seed.
    How to recognise it
    The reported final loss or the stopping epoch changes noticeably between identical runs with different shuffles, or training stopped in an epoch where the full-data loss was still falling.
    How to fix it
    Evaluate on the full training set or a fixed validation set once per epoch, and stop only after several evaluations in a row without improvement beyond a tolerance, as scikit-learn's n_iter_no_change and tol settings do.

  4. Feeding the data in its stored order instead of shuffling it.

    Why it causes problems
    If rows are sorted by class, date or customer, each batch represents one slice of the data and its gradient points towards fitting that slice. The parameters swing from slice to slice, and the final model is biased towards whatever came last.
    How to recognise it
    The loss curve repeats the same shape every epoch, or evaluation results depend on where in the epoch training was stopped.
    How to fix it
    Shuffle the training rows before every epoch. scikit-learn's SGD estimators do this by default; in other libraries check the shuffle setting of the data loader. For a stream that cannot be shuffled as a whole, shuffle within a buffer and avoid ending training in the middle of a sorted block.

  5. Changing the batch size and leaving the learning rate where it was.

    Why it causes problems
    With an averaged loss, a batch eight times larger makes one eighth as many updates per epoch, each about the same size, so the model covers less ground in the same number of epochs. Going the other way, a much smaller batch makes every step noisier and can destabilise a rate that was safe.
    How to recognise it
    After the batch size was raised to use more hardware, the loss after the same number of epochs is clearly higher than before, although each epoch now finishes faster.
    How to fix it
    Treat the two settings as a pair. As a starting point scale the learning rate in proportion to the batch size and ramp up to it over the first epochs, as the Facebook large-minibatch paper does, then confirm with a short sweep.

Requirements

  • Compute the loss from probabilities clipped to the range 1e-15 to 1 − 1e-15 so that the logarithm never receives 0.
  • Use one training function for all runs, with the batch size and the decay as arguments.
  • Shuffle the row order at the start of every epoch with a seeded random generator, so that the run can be repeated.
  • Always report the loss on all ten rows, not the loss of the last mini-batch.
  • Compare every run against a reference optimum obtained by running batch gradient descent for 20,000 steps.

Expected behaviour

At zero weights the loss is ln⁡2=0.6931\ln 2 = 0.6931ln2=0.6931 and the gradient is (−0.475,0)(-0.475, 0)(−0.475,0). The analytic and numerical gradients at (0.5,−1)(0.5, -1)(0.5,−1) agree to six decimals: (−0.014541,0.082593)(-0.014541, 0.082593)(−0.014541,0.082593).

The reference optimum is w=1.3534w = 1.3534w=1.3534, b=−3.7219b = -3.7219b=−3.7219 with a loss of 0.4335. After 200 epochs, batch gradient descent is close (loss 0.4351). Mini-batches of 2 at a constant rate make five times as many updates and end worse: 0.5386 with random.Random(0), and anywhere from 0.44 to 0.76 with other seeds. With the decaying rate the same mini-batches reach 0.4340.

After 20 epochs, batch gradient descent on raw hours is at 0.5350, and on centred hours at 0.4349.

Hint 1

At w = 0 and b = 0 every prediction is 0.5, so the errors are +0.5 for the students who failed and −0.5 for those who passed. You can check the starting gradient by hand.

Hint 2

If the constant-rate mini-batch run looks broken, print its loss every 20 epochs. It is not diverging. It is bouncing around the minimum.

Hint 3

Centring changes the intercept that the model needs, not its predictions. Think about how far b has to travel from 0 in each version.

Show solution
python
import math
import random

hours  = [0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 2.5, 3.0, 3.5, 4.0, 4.5, 5.0]
passed = [0, 0, 0, 1, 0, 1, 0, 1, 1, 1]

def predict(w, b, x):
    return 1 / (1 + math.exp(-(w * x + b)))

def log_loss(w, b, xs):
    total = 0.0
    for x, y in zip(xs, passed):
        p = min(max(predict(w, b, x), 1e-15), 1 - 1e-15)   # keep log() away from 0
        total -= y * math.log(p) + (1 - y) * math.log(1 - p)
    return total / len(xs)

def gradient(w, b, xs, rows):
    errors = [predict(w, b, xs[i]) - passed[i] for i in rows]
    grad_w = sum(e * xs[i] for e, i in zip(errors, rows)) / len(rows)
    return grad_w, sum(errors) / len(rows)

def train(xs, lr, epochs, batch_size, decay=0.0):
    rng = random.Random(0)
    w, b, updates = 0.0, 0.0, 0
    for _ in range(epochs):
        order = list(range(len(xs)))
        rng.shuffle(order)
        for start in range(0, len(xs), batch_size):
            gw, gb = gradient(w, b, xs, order[start:start + batch_size])
            step = lr / (1 + decay * updates)
            w, b, updates = w - step * gw, b - step * gb, updates + 1
    return w, b

everything = range(len(hours))
print(f"start: loss={log_loss(0, 0, hours):.4f} gradient={gradient(0, 0, hours, everything)}")

h = 1e-6
gw, gb = gradient(0.5, -1.0, hours, everything)
num_w = (log_loss(0.5 + h, -1.0, hours) - log_loss(0.5 - h, -1.0, hours)) / (2 * h)
num_b = (log_loss(0.5, -1.0 + h, hours) - log_loss(0.5, -1.0 - h, hours)) / (2 * h)
print(f"check: analytic=({gw:.6f}, {gb:.6f}) numeric=({num_w:.6f}, {num_b:.6f})")

def report(label, xs, w, b):
    print(f"{label:<34} w={w:.4f} b={b:.4f} loss={log_loss(w, b, xs):.4f}")

report("batch, 200 epochs", hours, *train(hours, 0.5, 200, 10))
report("batches of 2, constant rate", hours, *train(hours, 0.5, 200, 2))
report("batches of 2, decaying rate", hours, *train(hours, 0.5, 200, 2, decay=0.01))
report("batch, 20 epochs, raw hours", hours, *train(hours, 0.5, 20, 10))
centred = [x - sum(hours) / len(hours) for x in hours]
report("batch, 20 epochs, centred hours", centred, *train(centred, 0.5, 20, 10))
report("reference (20,000 batch steps)", hours, *train(hours, 0.5, 20000, 10))
text
start: loss=0.6931 gradient=(-0.475, 0.0)
check: analytic=(-0.014541, 0.082593) numeric=(-0.014541, 0.082593)
batch, 200 epochs                  w=1.2254 b=-3.3216 loss=0.4351
batches of 2, constant rate        w=1.2184 b=-4.5342 loss=0.5386
batches of 2, decaying rate        w=1.2751 b=-3.5254 loss=0.4340
batch, 20 epochs, raw hours        w=0.4891 b=-0.9819 loss=0.5350
batch, 20 epochs, centred hours    w=1.2227 b=-0.0000 loss=0.4349
reference (20,000 batch steps)     w=1.3534 b=-3.7219 loss=0.4335

Step 1. With all predictions at 0.5, the gradient for www is 110(0.5×27.5−18.5)=−0.475\frac{1}{10}(0.5 \times 27.5 - 18.5) = -0.475101​(0.5×27.5−18.5)=−0.475, where 27.5 is the sum of all hours and 18.5 the sum of the hours of those who passed. The gradient for bbb is 0 because five passed and five failed.

Step 3. The batch run follows the exact gradient and is within 0.002 of the optimum. The mini-batch run makes 1,000 updates instead of 200, but a gradient from 2 rows is a rough estimate, and at a constant rate of 0.5 each one throws the parameters a long way. The run ends wherever the last few batches left it: over 40 different seeds the final loss ranges from 0.44 to 0.76. Dividing the rate by (1+0.01t)(1 + 0.01t)(1+0.01t) shrinks it to a sixth of its starting value by update 500 and to an eleventh by the end, so early updates travel fast and late ones average the noise away. With the decay, all 40 seeds end between 0.4338 and 0.4342.

Step 4. On raw hours the optimum needs b=−3.72b = -3.72b=−3.72 while the gradient for bbb starts at 0, and any change in www shifts every prediction, so the two parameters have to be corrected in turns along a narrow valley. Centring removes that coupling. The hours are symmetric around their mean of 2.75 and exactly half the students passed, so the best intercept for the centred model is b=0b = 0b=0, which is where it starts, and only www has to move. Twenty updates then do what two hundred did before.

Check your answer

  • Is your loss at w = 0, b = 0 equal to 0.6931, the natural log of 2?
  • Do your analytic and numerical gradients at (0.5, −1) agree to at least five decimals?
  • Does your reference optimum predict a pass probability of 0.5 at 2.75 hours, which is −b divided by w?
  • Can you explain why the constant-rate mini-batch run ends worse than batch despite five times as many updates?
  • Does centring the hours leave the fitted slope near 1.35 and move the intercept to about 0?

Exercise 2

Diagnose four gradient descent runs from their loss logs

AnalysisIntermediateAbout 35 min (estimate)Hypothetical scenario

A colleague fits a linear regression by gradient descent on mean squared error. It predicts delivery minutes from two features: route distance in kilometres (1 to 15) and parcel weight in grams (100 to 5,000). There are 40 training rows and every run starts from zero weights. The data are synthetic, and the logs below come from really running each configuration. The rows themselves are not listed, so every question below is to be answered from the logs and the figures given here. The least-squares solution has a training MSE of 3.668, with an intercept of 6.00, 2.60 minutes per km and 0.00186 minutes per gram.

Run A. Raw features, batch gradient descent, learning rate 0.001. Loss after epochs 0 to 4:

text
898.5    2.59e+11    9.2e+19    3.27e+28    1.16e+37

Run B. Raw features, batch gradient descent, learning rate 0.0000001.

Epoch01235101001,0005,000
Loss898.49739.09614.49517.09381.44230.53168.23167.13162.33

After 5,000 epochs the weights are: intercept 0.0035, km 0.055, grams 0.0087.

Run C. Both features standardised, batch gradient descent, learning rate 0.1.

Epoch0125101519202122233040
Loss898.49573.60366.8898.0113.754.763.8543.7883.7453.7183.7003.6693.668

Run D. Both features standardised, one row per update (40 updates per epoch), learning rate 0.1. Loss on all 40 rows at the end of each epoch:

Epoch0123456789102030
Loss898.499.785.164.823.785.527.873.856.726.787.716.127.93

Between epochs 10 and 30 the loss ranges from 3.84 to 7.94.

  1. For each run, say whether it is healthy. If it is not, name the pattern, its cause and the first change you would make.
  2. Run B is still at 162 after 5,000 epochs. Using the weights given, explain which parameters have barely moved, and why raising the learning rate is not an available fix.
  3. Apply this rule to Run C: stop after the first epoch whose relative loss improvement is below 1%. At which epoch does training stop, and how far above the minimum is the loss there?
  4. Run D reaches 9.78 after one epoch, while Run C needs twelve epochs to get below that. Explain why D is ahead early and why it never settles, and give two changes that would let it settle.

Requirements

  • Tie every diagnosis to a specific feature of the log, such as the factor by which the loss changes between epochs.
  • Estimate the largest stable learning rate for the raw features from the size of the gram values, to within a factor of two.
  • Show the two relative improvements that decide the stopping epoch in task 3.
  • Name changes that address the cause you identified, not generic advice.

Expected behaviour

A complete answer identifies Run A as divergence from a learning rate thousands of times above the stable limit, Run B as a crawl caused by unscaled features with the rate already at its limit, Run C as a healthy run that the 1% rule stops at epoch 22, and Run D as a noise floor caused by single-row updates at a constant rate. It gives a stable limit near 0.0000001 for the raw features, a loss of 3.718 at the stopping epoch (about 1.4% above the minimum), and two workable fixes for Run D.

Hint 1

For a feature with values around 100 to 5,000, the curvature along its weight is twice the mean of its squared values. The learning rate must stay below 2 divided by the largest curvature.

Hint 2

Relative improvement is the previous loss minus the current loss, divided by the previous loss.

Hint 3

Count the updates. After one epoch Run C has made 1 update and Run D has made 40.

Show solution

Run A: divergence. The loss is multiplied by roughly 3.6×1083.6 \times 10^83.6×108 every epoch, the signature of a learning rate above the stable limit. The curvature along the grams weight is twice the mean of grams squared. With values between 100 and 5,000 the mean square is about 9 million, so the curvature is about 1.9×1071.9 \times 10^71.9×107 and the limit is 2/(1.9×107)≈1.1×10−72 / (1.9 \times 10^7) \approx 1.1 \times 10^{-7}2/(1.9×107)≈1.1×10−7. A rate of 0.001 is roughly 9,000 times too high. Dividing the rate by 10 would not help. The first change is to standardise the features.

Run B: a crawl with the rate at its limit. A rate of 10−710^{-7}10−7 sits just under the limit, so it cannot be raised. The loss falls quickly for about ten epochs, which is the grams weight settling along the steep direction, and then flattens at 168 and loses only 6 more in 4,900 epochs. The intercept is at 0.0035 where 6.00 is needed and the km weight is at 0.055 where 2.60 is needed. Their curvatures are 2 and about 113, so at this rate each step closes about two ten-millionths and one hundred-thousandth of their gaps. The grams weight has moved to 0.0087, well above its final 0.00186, because it is the only parameter able to move and is standing in for the other two. The fix is the same as for Run A: standardise, then choose the rate again.

Run C: healthy. After standardising, the loss above the minimum shrinks by a steady factor of about 0.64 per epoch and flattens at 3.668, the least-squares value. For the stopping rule: epoch 20 to 21 improves by (3.788−3.745)/3.788=1.1%(3.788 - 3.745) / 3.788 = 1.1\%(3.788−3.745)/3.788=1.1%, so training continues, and epoch 21 to 22 improves by (3.745−3.718)/3.745=0.7%(3.745 - 3.718) / 3.745 = 0.7\%(3.745−3.718)/3.745=0.7%, so training stops after epoch 22 at 3.718. That is 0.050 above the minimum, or 1.4%. Here the rule works because scaling has left no slow direction. Applied to Run B, the same rule stops at epoch 20 with the loss at 174.

Run D: a noise floor. After one epoch D has made 40 updates and C has made 1, and far from the minimum even a one-row gradient points roughly the right way, so D is ahead. Near the minimum the full gradient is close to zero but each row's own gradient is not, because every row has a residual. At a constant rate of 0.1 each update moves the parameters by an amount that does not shrink, so the loss wanders between 3.8 and 7.9 and never stays at 3.67. In our runs on the same data, each of these lets it settle:

  • Decay the learning rate. Dividing it by (1+0.02×updates)(1 + 0.02 \times \text{updates})(1+0.02×updates) keeps the same run at or below 3.68 from epoch 10 onwards.
  • Use a larger batch. With 8 rows per update and the same rate, the loss stays between 3.67 and 3.70 after epoch 10.
  • Use a smaller constant rate. At 0.01 with one row per update, the loss stays between 3.67 and 3.68 after epoch 10, at the price of a slower start (172 after the first epoch).

Check your answer

  • Did you identify unscaled features, not just a wrong learning rate, as the cause of both Run A and Run B?
  • Is your estimate of the largest stable learning rate for the raw features close to 0.0000001?
  • Did you find that the 1% rule stops Run C after epoch 22 at a loss of 3.718?
  • Can you say why Run D is faster than Run C at first and worse than Run C at the end?
  • Did you propose at least two of these for Run D - a decaying rate, a larger batch, a smaller rate?

6Curated resources

Chosen for accuracy and usefulness, not search rank. Time figures are estimates.

  • Linear regression: Gradient descent | Machine Learning | Google for Developers (opens in a new tab)

    Google for Developers (Machine Learning Crash Course)

    CourseBeginnerFreeAbout 45 minutes (estimate)

    What it teaches
    Gradient descent on a small fuel-efficiency dataset with the weight, bias and loss shown for each of the first iterations, loss curves, convergence and the convex loss surface of a linear model. The neighbouring pages cover loss functions and the learning rate, batch size and epoch settings, each with check-your-understanding questions.
    When to use it
    If this lesson moved too fast and you want a second, slower pass over the same ideas before writing any code.

  • 12.3. Gradient Descent — Dive into Deep Learning 1.0.3 documentation (opens in a new tab)

    Dive into Deep Learning (Zhang, Lipton, Li and Smola)

    BookIntermediateFreeAbout 1 hour (estimate)

    What it teaches
    Why a step against the gradient lowers the loss, using a Taylor expansion, with runnable experiments for learning rates that are too small and too large, a non-convex example with local minima, and an introduction to Newton's method and preconditioning as ways of matching the step to the curvature.
    When to use it
    When you want the mathematics behind the three learning-rate regimes in this lesson, or a bridge to second-order methods.

  • An overview of gradient descent optimization algorithms (opens in a new tab)

    Sebastian Ruder (ruder.io)

    ArticleIntermediateFreeAbout 1 hour (estimate)

    What it teaches
    The three gradient descent variants and their trade-offs in one place, the challenges they share, and then the optimizers built to address them: momentum, Nesterov, Adagrad, Adadelta, RMSprop and Adam, with the update rule and the motivation for each.
    When to use it
    After this lesson, when you meet an optimizer name in a framework and want to know what it changes about the plain update.

  • CS231n Deep Learning for Computer Vision: Learning (course notes) (opens in a new tab)

    Stanford University (CS231n)

    CourseIntermediateFreeAbout 1 hour (estimate)

    What it teaches
    How to supervise a training run: gradient checks, sanity checks before training, what loss curves look like at low, high and good learning rates, the ratio of update size to weight size, learning-rate annealing and hyperparameter search.
    When to use it
    When a real training run misbehaves and you need a checklist of what to plot and what each plot means.

  • 1.5. Stochastic Gradient Descent — scikit-learn 1.9.1 documentation (opens in a new tab)

    scikit-learn developers

    DocumentationIntermediateFreeAbout 40 minutes (estimate)

    What it teaches
    How scikit-learn's SGDClassifier and SGDRegressor apply stochastic gradient descent: the available loss functions and penalties, the stopping criteria, the learning-rate schedules with their formulas, and practical tips on scaling, shuffling and the number of iterations.
    When to use it
    When you want to train a linear model by SGD on real data without writing the loop, or need to know what a parameter such as eta0 or n_iter_no_change does.
